2.text: The later the season, the better is the meat, because the animals are no

3.text: longer worried by insects, and can feed undisturbed. The meat of young

4.text: animals killed in midsummer is so lean and tasteless, that it is really only fit

5.text: for dog-food. The buck-skins are valued for summer bedding and as the

6.text: best material for curried leather. The fawn-skins, on the contrary, are poor,

7.text: since the hunter cannot choose his own time for killing. Only the poorest

8.text: people use them for garments, while all others buy fawn-skins from the rein-

10.text: At the places where the migrating reindeer crossed the Kolyma and its

11.text: affluents, the Yukaghir inhabitants used to set long rows of snares on both

12.text: banks of the river, spreading them out on the trees and among the bushes.

13.text: These were still more efficient than hunting on the water; but bush and forest

14.text: on the Middle Anadyr are too scanty to allow of this method of hunting.

15.text: At the mouth of the Kolyma, where the migration of reindeer still continues

16.text: to some extent, a few score reindeer are killed every summer on the water,

17.text: and in some places single snares are still spread on the reindeer-trail.

18.text: The frame of the kayak used by the Chukchee for hunting reindeer on

19.text: the rivers (Fig. 47, b) is similar to the common Eskimo form, but it is covered
19.note: Printed italic 'b'; machine draft misread it as digit '6'. Verified at 2x zoom.

20.text: with reindeer-skin instead of seal-skin. The manhole in the middle remains

21.text: open, because there is no need of making it water-tight for use on the river.

22.text: The kayak is employed because of its lightness as compared to that of the

23.text: wooden canoes of the Russianized Yukaghir. The type of the Maritime Chukchee

24.text: kayak is represented in Fig. 47, c. The double paddle (Fig. 47, a) is similar

25.text: to that of the Yukaghir, and has a stem that is straight or somewhat curved,

26.text: with blades in the shape of a poplar-leaf. In shallow waters two slender

27.text: sticks about 150 cm. long and 1 cm. thick are used, both with the dug-out

28.text: and with the skin canoe, for punting. The sporadic occurrence of the kayak

29.text: all along the Asiatic shore is very curious. It exists on the Arctic, then
